analysis.one_liner: Caps federal student loan interest rates at 3% for new and consolidation loans.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap federal student loan interest at 3% died in committee without a single hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Higher Education Act so that federal student loans first disbursed on or after July 1, 2024 — including Stafford, Unsubsidized Stafford, and PLUS loans — could not charge more than 3% interest [S2]. It also capped new federal consolidation loans at 3%, no matter what rates the underlying loans carried [S2]. It was introduced on August 30, 2024, near the end of the two-year congressional session, and was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee [S1]. It never advanced from there.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and families taking out new federal loans would pay far less interest than under current formulas, which have set undergraduate loan rates around 6-8% in recent years. Borrowers with existing loans could also benefit by consolidating into a new 3% loan, since the bill says the consolidation rate applies regardless of the rates on the original loans [S2]. Lower interest means more of each payment goes to paying down the loan itself, saving borrowers money over the life of the loan.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the interest rate on new Federal Direct Stafford, Unsubsidized Stafford, and PLUS loans at 3% for loans first disbursed on or after July 1, 2024, overriding the rate formulas in current law [S2].

Caps new Federal Direct Consolidation Loans at 3%, regardless of the interest rates on the loans being consolidated, which would let existing borrowers with higher-rate loans effectively reset their rate by consolidating [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government — ultimately taxpayers — would collect much less interest on its loan portfolio. Interest income on federal student loans helps offset defaults, loan forgiveness costs, and program administration, so a deep rate cut shifts those costs to the general taxpayer. In a low-interest-rate era this cost would be modest; if market rates were high, the subsidy cost would be large.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers via the loan program

drawbacks.text: The 3% cap is a fixed number no matter what interest rates the government itself pays to borrow, so the cost to taxpayers of the subsidy grows when market rates rise, and the bill contains no mechanism to adjust the cap [S2].

The cap applies only to new loans and new consolidation loans, so most existing borrowers would get relief only if they went through the consolidation process, which resets repayment terms and can forfeit some borrower benefits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to borrowers is real and substantial — a rate cut from roughly 7% to 3% on a typical loan saves thousands of dollars over its life. The main cost is fiscal: the Treasury forgoes interest income and taxpayers absorb the difference. The bill is a blunt instrument (a fixed 3% with no adjustment for rate conditions, and no help for borrowers who don't consolidate), but its core trade-off is straightforward: cheaper loans for students, paid for by the federal budget.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final months of the session and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Moskowitz introduced the Student Loan Interest Cap Act on August 30, 2024, joined by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna [S1].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced, and no further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S4].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Republicans, in the roughly four months before the 118th Congress ended [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal student loan borrowers gained nothing, since the cap never took effect; the Treasury keeps collecting interest at the existing statutory rates, and the committee's inaction preserved the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury, which keeps collecting loan interest

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with a Democratic sponsor and only two cosponsors, it had no path to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat with two Republican cosponsors, but no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so there was no recorded party split.

industries.note: The government would collect far less interest on new and consolidation loans, a direct budget cost to taxpayers. That cost is the flip side of the savings going to borrowers.

If federal loans cost 3%, far fewer borrowers would need to refinance high-rate federal debt with private lenders, shrinking that market. This industry losing would run alongside borrowers' interests.
The bill changes interest rates but leaves the existing servicing structure untouched, keeping private servicers as the permanent intermediaries between borrowers and the federal loan program.
